item.title: [LU-20591] Support iterating OSD objects via llapi
item.description:
It will be very useful if we can do that for some obvious reasons:

  • Better policy engine - it can just iterate the objects on the MDTs to make a decision which files should be moved
  • Rebalance OSTs - by iterating objects on fully occupied OSTs, it can figure out which large objects should be migrated, especially with this proposed Stripe Replacement feature 

The work seems straightforward. I will burn some tokens and get some patches.

vkuznetsov since you are the "lipe find man" I think it's important for you to get involved in this conversation.
jinshanx, I've written an overall design doc (what my LUG presentation was based on) and the tracking ticket LU-20462 was created for this work. I will share the design in the wiki next week
Hi. I'm currently working on a similar scanner for LU-20462 with some differences in the design. I'm happy to share what we have if that's useful. Thanks.

It seems LU-20462 is more advanced solution since it leverages multiple threads scanning and zero-copy from kernel space to user space. hnishida adilger can you share the design doc?

My current implementation is straightforward and should be fast (I haven't tested it yet but there is no reason to be slow) because it only scans inode table by default without reading extra EA. It will be pretty easy to change it to zero-copy if necessary. It won't be a huge amount of data anyways.
Here's mine: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/d38362e0-7724-4fe1-8469-8be7f94769c6
Do you parallelize a target scanning with multiple threads? If we're able to do that, that would be very interesting.
No, our OSD scanner is single threaded, while the userland scanner is multi-threaded. However, the OSD one fans out the per-object work behind the enumerator: 2 workers hold ~900k obj/s on ldiskfs.
I have parallelized our OSD scanner. Please take a look at https://github.com/scopedog/lfu

What does the `threads` mean in the benchmark results, for example:

ldiskfs · warm 1,818,270 (1 thread)
4,545,675 (-j 4)		 6,873,185 (1 thread)
17,392,147 (4 threads)		 3.8× Option 2

What does `4 threads` mean in the text?

Our parallelization shards the object-ID space (inode numbers on ldiskfs, dnode numbers on ZFS).
"N threads": N private osd_otable_it iterators, one per kernel thread, each over a disjoint range. That needs a new DOIF_PARALLEL flag — without it the OSD allows only one otable iterator per device.

thanks for the explanation. How do you know the highest inode and dnode numbers so that you can split the workload well distributed?

For ldiskfs, it's straightforward by scanning it in block groups. It's much more difficult for zfs though. And we can't make it OSD agnostic.

ldiskfs is already fast enough with single thread.

> How do you know the highest inode and dnode numbers?

We actually don't know the highest numbers and we don't use them. Threads take fixed-size chunks of the object-number space from a shared atomic cursor. A chunk whose load()/next() returns 1 found nothing at or after its start; chunks are handed out in increasing order, so every later chunk is empty too — that thread sets a global done and the others finish their current chunk. No size query, no maximum, same logic on both backends.
 
You're right that static equal ranges distribute badly, and we hit exactly that: on a young MDT 2M inodes sat in 62 of ~1000 groups, so an even split leaves N−1 threads idle. With dynamic chunks a thread that lands on an unallocated region walks the UNINIT groups in microseconds and takes the next chunk. On ldiskfs it's worth making the chunk a multiple of inodes-per-group, so shards are group-aligned and two threads never hold the same group bitmap.

> we can't make it OSD agnostic

The sharding rides on load(hash)/store() — the position cookies both OSDs already implement for scrub checkpointing. The consumer loop is identical on both: init(DOIF_PARALLEL) → load(start-1) → next()/rec() until store() >= end → fini(). It never interprets the cookie, only compares and advances, so "inode number" vs "dnode number" never reaches it. That's running on both backends today.

One osd-zfs quirk found doing it: load(hash) resumes at hash + 1 because dmu_object_next() returns objects strictly after *objectp, so a checkpoint/resume silently skips one object. Private iterators start the search at hash instead.

> ldiskfs is already fast enough with single thread

Agreed, and our numbers say the same. With block parsing one private thread is 6.87M obj/s warm; cold — the regime that actually sizes a scan — it is 1,119,013 against 1,420,664 at four threads, only 1.27×, because one thread already reaches ~78% of an NVMe stripe and four reach 99%. Parallelism is not what ldiskfs needs.

ZFS is where it pays: 97,304 singleton → 410,529 at eight threads cold, 4.2×, and that is what makes the in-kernel scanner ~1.8× the userspace one there. So the backend that's harder to shard is the one that needs it — which is why the range-free chunking above is the part worth keeping.

hnishida thanks for the explanation. I will pause my work and let you continue working on your project.

I'd suggest that you land your patches phase by phase. In the initial phase, we can just iterate the objects on the server side, which is already useful. The second phase could move to client side support but I believe we will have to have multiple clients to collaborate with each other otherwise the network will become a bottleneck.

Look forward to your patches.

jinshanx If you are interested, please join LU-20462. We are currently working on userspace scanners (hopefully for 2.18) but will also support the kernel side (for 2.19). If you have an idea to expand them, please let us know.
please let me know if you need anything from me. I have unlimited amount of tokens to burn.
